Book Two: The nature of the animal soul, its substantiality, and its partial independence from matter
passage-en-00173

We answer that “plant soul” may mean one of three things. It may mean the specific soul that belongs to plants and not animals. Or it may mean the general principle shared by plant, animal, and human souls: the source of nourishment, growth, and reproduction. Or it may mean the soul’s particular power that produces these three plant functions.
Book Two: The nature of the animal soul, its substantiality, and its partial independence from matter
passage-en-00174

If it means the first, then the specifically plant soul does not exist as an actual, separate kind in an animal. This is like saying that a weak shade of black exists as a separate actual thing inside a deeper black.
Book Two: The nature of the animal soul, its substantiality, and its partial independence from matter
passage-en-00175

If it means the second, then a general principle produces only a general effect, just as writing in general comes from a writer in general. Plant matter is not made fully actual by a separate, general plant soul. A natural kind or general feature cannot exist by itself apart from the conditions of its existence. If matter is not made fully actual by a general plant principle, then the animal soul does not arrive in something already constituted in its own right.
Book Two: The nature of the animal soul, its substantiality, and its partial independence from matter
passage-en-00176

If it means the third, then the matter is not as those unfamiliar with theoretical philosophy imagine: the power of growth first produces an animal body, and then the animal soul arrives and takes control of it, making the growing power one of its tools. That is like a craftsperson deliberately making a tool and then using it. The plant power is one power of a soul that has other powers too. It cannot exist before that soul; otherwise the soul’s instrument would be in use before the soul that uses it. The plant power is a branch of the animal soul and cannot exist fully apart from it. In the same way, the animal soul is not fully actual in a being with a rational soul except through that rational soul. As we shall see, each of us has one soul, and all the other powers are effects of it and branches that spread through the organs. This is the view widely held by the leading philosophers of later times.
Book Two: The nature of the animal soul, its substantiality, and its partial independence from matter
passage-en-00177

My settled view is that the soul is all the powers together: their single, unified source and their beginning and end. The same is true of every higher power in relation to the lower powers it uses, whether it uses them in sequence or together. The powers come one after another in time; what comes earlier in time is later in rank and dignity. The soul in us—or in any animal—gathers the elements of the body, combines them, and shapes them into a body fit to be its own. It nourishes and grows that body, makes it an individual through nourishment and a member of its kind through reproduction, preserves its health, wards off illness, restores the right temperament when it has been disturbed, and keeps the body in its proper order. While the soul is present, outside changes do not overcome the body.
Book Two: The nature of the animal soul, its substantiality, and its partial independence from matter
passage-en-00178

If the soul were not also the source of the plant and natural functions in the body, as it is of perception and animal actions, the body would not keep its health. It would fall apart under the pressure of outside conditions. This is also why feelings and beliefs that please or hurt us affect the body and strengthen or weaken the powers of growth. It is not belief by itself that changes the body. It must be accompanied by a change in the subtle materials that run through the body, brought about by joy or grief. These, too, are states of the soul. They first change the state and temperament of the vital spirit, then, through the powers, the state and temperament of the denser body. Rational joy makes bodily powers—especially the power of growth—stronger and more active. Rational grief weakens them, leaving them feeble and sluggish until their activity is impaired and the body’s temperament is damaged. This strongly shows that the soul’s action and governance extend through the body’s furthest and densest material layers, even though its own essence belongs to a subtler and higher level.
Book Two: The nature of the animal soul, its substantiality, and its partial independence from matter
passage-en-00179

The animal soul—and likewise the human soul—gathers the perceptive and plant powers, together with their immediate and more distant subjects. It is therefore a perfection of a subject that cannot become actual without it. It also completes and brings about a kind of thing. Things that differ in their souls differ in their essential kind, not just in temporary features.
Book Two: The nature of the animal soul, its substantiality, and its partial independence from matter
passage-en-00180

The plant powers found in plants differ in nature and kind from the plant powers found in animals. In neither case are these powers accidents, as some have supposed. They are substances: actual in plants, but potential in animals. “Potential” here does not mean that they have only a preparatory possibility. Their potentiality is like the way intelligible forms are present in the simple intellect as a unified, active capacity.
Book Two: The nature of the animal soul, its substantiality, and its partial independence from matter
passage-en-00181
IV. The powers of the soul that branch out through the body
Book Two: The nature of the animal soul, its substantiality, and its partial independence from matter
passage-en-00182

In The Healing, Avicenna says that the powers of the soul fall first into three kinds. The first is the plant soul: the first perfection of a natural body with organs, insofar as it grows, develops, and reproduces. The second is the animal soul: the first perfection of a natural body with organs, insofar as it perceives particular things and moves by choice. The third is the human soul: the first perfection of a natural body with organs, insofar as it understands universal things and acts through reflective choice and judgment. Each kind has degrees, from greater to lesser perfection. The plant soul has three powers. The nutritive power changes another body into something like the body it belongs to, attaches it to that body, and makes it similar to itself, replacing what has worn away.
Book Two: The nature of the animal soul, its substantiality, and its partial independence from matter
passage-en-00183

The growth power increases the body by adding material that has been made like it, in proportion across its length, width, and depth, until the body reaches its full growth. The reproductive power takes from the body a material that is potentially like it. With the help of other bodies, it shapes and forms this material until it becomes actually like the body that produced it.
Book Two: The nature of the animal soul, its substantiality, and its partial independence from matter
passage-en-00184

By its first division, the animal soul has two powers: a power that moves and a power that perceives. The moving power is either a motive power, which urges the animal to move, or an active power, which carries out the movement. The motive power is a final cause—the noblest of the four kinds of cause, as you know. It is the power of desire, which is connected to the imaginative power discussed below. When an image of something wanted or avoided takes shape in imagination, desire prompts the other moving power to act. Desire has two branches. One is appetite, which urges movement towards something imagined as necessary or useful for preserving the animal’s life, in pursuit of pleasure. The other is anger, which urges movement to repel something imagined as harmful or destructive, in pursuit of dominance.
Book Two: The nature of the animal soul, its substantiality, and its partial independence from matter
passage-en-00185

The active moving power is a force that arises in the nerves and muscles. It contracts the muscles, drawing the tendons and ligaments attached to the limbs towards their point of origin; or it relaxes them or stretches them, moving the tendons and ligaments away from that point.
Book Two: The nature of the animal soul, its substantiality, and its partial independence from matter
passage-en-00186

The perceptive power is divided into two kinds: one perceives from outside, the other from within. The external powers are the five senses—or eight, if touch is divided into its parts. Avicenna then defines each of the external senses, and when he comes to touch he says that it is a power located in the nerves of the skin and flesh throughout the body. It perceives what comes into contact with it and affects it by opposition—either changing its temperament or disrupting the way its parts are arranged.
Book Two: The nature of the animal soul, its substantiality, and its partial independence from matter
passage-en-00187

Some people seem to treat touch not as one kind of sense, but as a general power containing four, or even more, powers spread through the skin. One detects the opposition between hot and cold; another, between wet and dry; a third, between hard and soft; and a fourth, between rough and smooth. Because all four work through one instrument, they may seem to be a single power in their own right.
Book Two: The nature of the animal soul, its substantiality, and its partial independence from matter
passage-en-00188

Avicenna then explains the inner powers in a summary that makes his account easier to follow. The perceptive power either perceives particular things or understands universal ones. Particular things are perceived either by the external senses, already described, or by the inner senses. An inner sense may only perceive, or it may both perceive and work with what it perceives.
Book Two: The nature of the animal soul, its substantiality, and its partial independence from matter
passage-en-00189

If it only perceives, it may perceive particular images or particular meanings. By particular images I mean, for example, the image formed of Zayd or ʿAmr. By particular meanings I mean perceiving that one person is a friend and another an enemy. The power that perceives particular images is called the common sense: all the images received from the external senses come together in it. The power that perceives particular meanings is called estimation. Each of these two powers has a storehouse. The common sense’s storehouse is imagination; estimation’s is memory. These are four powers in all.
Book Two: The nature of the animal soul, its substantiality, and its partial independence from matter
passage-en-00190

The power that works with what it perceives combines and separates the images stored in those two storehouses. It might combine a human shape with a bird’s, or imagine a mountain made of emerald or a sea of quicksilver. When the animal’s power of estimation uses this faculty, it is called imagination; when the rational power uses it, it is called thought.
Book Two: The nature of the animal soul, its substantiality, and its partial independence from matter
passage-en-00191

Avicenna and his followers say that the common sense and imagination are located in the front part of the brain. The power that combines and works with images is located in the middle part, as is estimation. Memory is located in the rear part of the brain. They do not mention the location of imagination, since it can be inferred from the fact that it is a storehouse.
Book Two: The nature of the animal soul, its substantiality, and its partial independence from matter
passage-en-00192

Some philosophers treat the animal soul as the whole set of these powers. Others identify the soul with estimation and treat all the other powers as subordinate to it. Each view has something right in it, as you will see. This is a brief account of the animal powers and their divisions. They are all carried by the vital spirit, whose substance resembles that of the heavens. The details of the rational soul’s powers will be discussed elsewhere. For now, I will set out the proofs for these powers, consider the objections, and answer them. First, however, I will explain how many kinds of difference there are among the soul’s actions. May God grant success.
Book Two: The nature of the animal soul, its substantiality, and its partial independence from matter
passage-en-00193
V. A principle for working out how many powers there are
Book Two: The nature of the animal soul, its substantiality, and its partial independence from matter
passage-en-00194

People commonly think that five kinds of difference explain why there are different powers and sources of action. First, things may differ in meaning. For example, “animal” includes the meanings of growing and sensing. Some therefore say that an animal is made up of matter and form: a plant-like body and a sensing soul. In the same way, they distinguish the nature of a plant by its bodily aspect, which comes from matter, and its plant life, which comes from form. They apply this pattern to everything made of matter and form. Second, actions may differ by being present or absent: movement and rest, knowledge and ignorance, certainty and doubt. Third, they may differ in strength: certainty and opinion in belief; greater or lesser desire in character; or larger and smaller bodies.
Book Two: The nature of the animal soul, its substantiality, and its partial independence from matter
passage-en-00195

Fourth, actions may differ in speed, as when someone grasps an idea at once rather than working it out step by step. Fifth, effects may differ in kind. They may share a close general kind, as when sight perceives black and white or taste perceives sweet and bitter; they may differ within more distant kinds, as when we perceive colors and sounds; or they may differ even more widely, as perception and movement do.
Book Two: The nature of the animal soul, its substantiality, and its partial independence from matter
passage-en-00196

With these distinctions in place, we can say that the first kind does not require several powers or several existences. A single, simple power can express several meanings without being divided either in itself or in its way of existing. For example, a separate intellect is both the one that understands and the one that is understood. Likewise, knowledge, power, will, and life—and all the other divine attributes—are truly said of the Necessary Being, exalted is He.
Book Two: The nature of the animal soul, its substantiality, and its partial independence from matter
passage-en-00197

The second kind does not require two powers or several sources of action either. An action may be present because its power exists, while its absence is due not to the loss of that power but to the absence of some condition needed for it to act. So the fact that an action sometimes occurs and sometimes does not is no proof that there must be more than one power.
Book Two: The nature of the animal soul, its substantiality, and its partial independence from matter
passage-en-00198

The third kind does not require several powers either. Otherwise, there would have to be a different power for every degree of greater or lesser strength, and so an infinite succession of distinct powers at successive moments. That is impossible. Here is why. An increase in strength is a continuous change in quality. It has an unbroken course in which we can imagine infinitely many points, each reached at some imagined instant and each having its own degree of strength. If each degree required a separate power, there would be infinitely many actual, distinct powers. Time and distance would then be made up of indivisible parts; an infinite series would be bounded by two limits; and a bodily power would be the source of infinitely many actions. All of these conclusions are impossible. The reason is more likely that one and the same power becomes stronger or weaker as the causes acting on it change, as its recipient or instrument changes, or as the instrument is sometimes impaired or tired and at other times sound and vigorous. The same account applies to differences in speed.
Book Two: The nature of the animal soul, its substantiality, and its partial independence from matter
passage-en-00199

As for the fifth kind of difference, some people claim that one power cannot independently produce effects that differ in kind, whether the kinds are close or far apart. On this view, a single power cannot both perceive and move; nor can one power perceive both inwardly and through the outer senses; nor can one power perceive colors, tastes, and smells. Each kind of effect must have its own power. This is the view Avicenna and his followers chose. But once you see that none of the differences listed above is, by itself, the source of the many powers, you can see that their explanation needs more care.
Book Two: The nature of the animal soul, its substantiality, and its partial independence from matter
passage-en-00200

Later commentators commonly say that philosophers such as Avicenna distinguish powers because each power is simple, and a simple thing can directly produce only one action. So, they say, one power may produce only one action as its primary effect, though it may produce others indirectly or by coincidence. For example, sight is one power that perceives color. The color it perceives may happen to be black or white. Imagination preserves an image stripped of matter, though not to the degree required for intellectual understanding; that image may happen to be a color, taste, smell, sound, heat, or something else. The intellect perceives things free of matter and its ties; what it perceives may be a heavenly sphere, an animal, a lifeless thing, a quality, a quantity, a position, a place, or any other category, general kind, or particular kind.
Book Two: The nature of the animal soul, its substantiality, and its partial independence from matter
passage-en-00201

This is not what Avicenna’s argument shows. The principle applies only to what is truly one in every respect. The powers are not like that: they have several possible aspects. Also, the argument that one thing of a given kind can produce only one effect of that kind would equally imply that one individual power can produce only one individual effect. That would mean the power of sight by which we perceive one patch of black is different from the power by which we perceive another patch of black. But if one individual power can be the source of many effects of the same kind, why could it not be the source of effects that differ in kind?
Book Two: The nature of the animal soul, its substantiality, and its partial independence from matter
passage-en-00202

The sound basis for distinguishing powers is not that famous principle. There are two proofs. The first is that one power can exist without another, which shows that they are distinct. For example, the power of growth can fail while the nutritive power remains, both in animals and in plants. So the growth power differs from the nutritive power. The reproductive power, too, may be absent while growth continues. The second proof is that two positive actions can oppose one another, as attraction opposes repulsion, or receiving something opposes holding on to it. Merely producing effects that differ in nature or kind does not prove that there are several powers. One power may act in different ways through its different aspects. The First Intellect, for example, gives rise to another intellect through the fullness and strength of its existence, and to a heavenly sphere through the limitation of its possible nature. Yet these active aspects cannot explain effects that differ only as separate individuals of the same kind do. Such individual differences require matter that can receive changing states brought about by accidental causes, such as motion—states not fixed in the thing from the beginning.
Book Two: The nature of the animal soul, its substantiality, and its partial independence from matter
passage-en-00203

Once these points are clear, no one can object: “Why not say that the soul itself performs all these actions, without having to suppose all these separate animal and other powers exist?” Even if we accept that the rational soul differs from the animal powers because it can reason without depending on bodily organs, while the animal powers act through the body, why not say that the animal power is one, and that perception and movement come from that same power? Even if we accept that they differ, why not say that the moving power is one, and that appetite and anger are one power that responds one way when it encounters pleasure and another when it encounters pain? Why not say, too, that one power perceives both external and internal things, and that a single external sense produces different actions through different organs?
Book Two: The nature of the animal soul, its substantiality, and its partial independence from matter
passage-en-00204

And why should the plant power differ from the animal power? Even if they differ, why not treat nourishment, growth, and reproduction as one power? At the beginning of an individual’s life, it supplies more material than is lost, so the body grows until it reaches its full size. Once it can no longer do that, it sends food to the moving body’s organs to nourish them. Any surplus no longer needed for nourishment and not used for growth is then put to another needed use: reproduction. The power continues to replace what is lost until it can no longer do so, and death follows. What we have already said answers these and similar objections. The case for several powers does not rest on the famous principle, as some have assumed, so the familiar counterexamples do not refute it.
Book Two: The nature of the animal soul, its substantiality, and its partial independence from matter
passage-en-00205

One counterexample is that the common sense perceives everything received by the external senses. If these perceptions differ, then the original argument has failed; if they do not, why could they not all come from one power? Another is that sight does not perceive just one kind of thing: it perceives black, white, and all the colors between them. If one power can perceive two kinds under one close general kind, why could it not perceive things that differ but fall under a more general kind? Also, a single power perceives shape and size, even if it does so by perceiving color first. So one power can perceive things that differ in kind, as well as things that differ within one kind.
Book Two: The nature of the animal soul, its substantiality, and its partial independence from matter
passage-en-00206

Another counterexample is that imagination perceives things that differ in kind, and the intellect perceives all things. So, the objectors conclude, the claim that one thing can produce only one effect is false, along with all the other objections of this sort.
Book Two: The nature of the animal soul, its substantiality, and its partial independence from matter
passage-en-00207

But, as you have seen, that principle applies only to a simple agent free of conditions, relations, and instruments. If an agent acts only when certain conditions are present, one and the same thing can produce many effects as different conditions join it. For example, nature is a simple power: it moves a body when the body is outside its natural place, and brings it to rest when it is in that place. Even the Active Intellect, which they say governs this elemental world, is a simple substance, yet it is the source of the events that occur here. The conditions and causes that prepare the matter differ.
Book Two: The nature of the animal soul, its substantiality, and its partial independence from matter
passage-en-00208

These objections and counterexamples come from a misunderstanding among later writers such as Abū al-Barakāt al-Baghdādī, Imam al-Rāzī, the author of al-Mawāqif, its commentator al-Sayyid al-Jurjānī, the commentator on Sharḥ al-Maqāṣid, al-Taftāzānī, and others who debate theology without probing deeply into rational inquiry or immersing themselves in philosophy.
Book Two: The nature of the animal soul, its substantiality, and its partial independence from matter
passage-en-00209

One of the arguments the author of al-Mulakhkhaṣ takes pride in, as though it had demolished the philosophers’ principle about the number of powers and the orderly arrangement of existence—where a natural whole gives rise to different effects and therefore requires different sources, all grounded in the unity of one soul—is this. He says: “We have a true and certain premise that no rational person doubts: whoever judges two things must perceive them. For judgment means affirming that something belongs to something, or denying it. That cannot happen without conceiving both sides. So the person making the judgment must conceive the two things being related, in order to judge one of them by the other.”
Book Two: The nature of the animal soul, its substantiality, and its partial independence from matter
passage-en-00210

“Now suppose we perceive a particular person and know that this individual belongs to the general kind “human being” but does not belong to the general kind “horse.” Whoever judges that this particular person is a human being rather than a horse must perceive both the individual being judged and the general description applied to it. So the power that perceives individual things must be the same power that understands general kinds.”
Book Two: The nature of the animal soul, its substantiality, and its partial independence from matter
passage-en-00211

He calls this a decisive insight that anyone with even a little understanding must accept, and wonders how earlier thinkers, despite their skill, could have missed it. I say: How can anyone who has searched so widely, written so much, and thought so deeply still have strayed so far from the truth and become so blind to what is plainly before him? He has failed to notice what the soul itself does. Some of its actions involve thought, some the senses, and some movement. The soul is the one that understands, imagines, smells, tastes, walks, grows, feeds itself, desires, feels anger, and more. It performs these many actions through different organs. It also acts and is affected without an organ: it forms an image of itself, understands first principles, and uses its organs. No organ lies between the soul and its use of an organ. What problem, then, is there in saying that the soul perceives or acts in some cases by itself and in others through an organ? It perceives this particular human being through sense, and understands what human beings have in common directly.
Book Two: The nature of the animal soul, its substantiality, and its partial independence from matter
passage-en-00212

It then judges what it perceived through sense by what it understood directly, saying, “This particular person is a human being.” Perhaps, after so long in a high religious office and such a wide reach of authority, the critic came to think that perceiving something through an organ means that the organ itself is the perceiver, while the soul knows nothing of what the organ perceives. That is a very poor assumption. It would mean that a single human being contains a crowd of separate perceivers, each limited to one kind of perception: one hears, another sees, a third tastes, a fourth smells, a fifth touches, a sixth imagines, a seventh estimates. The same would hold for movement: one power handles things, another attracts, another repels, another digests, another desires, and another feels anger.
Book Two: The nature of the animal soul, its substantiality, and its partial independence from matter
passage-en-00213

The same would be true of all the other powers. On this view, the soul would know nothing of these actions and reactions except its own nature and the qualities that belong to it. That is contrary to what we experience and what reason proves. In experience, each of us knows that we are the one who understands, imagines, smells, tastes, writes, moves, and sits. The proof is that the soul chooses to see, hear, and touch, and uses its particular organs to achieve general or particular aims. A particular aim is clear: someone may move in order to see a certain person. A general aim would be to go to a teacher to learn intellectual sciences. Whoever chooses to use a particular organ must perceive that organ.
Book Two: The nature of the animal soul, its substantiality, and its partial independence from matter
passage-en-00214

Reason also shows that the soul, not the sense or its organ, perceives the particular images received by the senses. Whoever perceives something must also be aware of itself in the act of perceiving, as we have already explained. A body, or a power that exists in a body, cannot perceive itself. Anything that returns to itself in its perception is therefore spiritual. These and similar arguments show that the human rational soul perceives both particulars and universals. It can judge a particular by a universal, just as it can judge one particular by another.
Book Two: The nature of the animal soul, its substantiality, and its partial independence from matter
passage-en-00215

The philosophers also use the first of the two proofs just mentioned to show that a natural power differs from an animal power. They say that we find a healthy organ carrying out natural functions while its sensory functions are impaired. The loss of sensation must be due either to the absence of a sensory power or to the organ’s inability to be affected by that power. If the first is true, the animal power must be something other than the natural power spread through the organ: the natural power is present even when the sensory power is not, so the two must differ. The second option is false, they say, because these bodies can receive heat and cold, tastes and smells. If the sensory power were present in an organ and these sensible qualities reached it, perception would follow: the perceiving power would be there, along with the form that produces sensation. The same kind of argument can show that the powers of hearing, sight, smell, and the other senses differ.
Book Two: The nature of the animal soul, its substantiality, and its partial independence from matter
passage-en-00216

For example, if the power of taste were the same as the power of smell, each should perceive what the other perceives, since the organ in each case can receive both taste and smell. But neither perceives what the other does, even when the relevant quality is present. So the two powers must differ in their nature.
Book Two: The nature of the animal soul, its substantiality, and its partial independence from matter
passage-en-00217

The author of al-Mabāḥith objects that perception does not necessarily follow just because the perceiving power and the thing perceived are both present in one place. Perception may depend on a condition that is missing. For example, the organ of touch may contain both the power of touch and the quality being touched, yet that power does not perceive the quality in the organ. Likewise, the power of sight exists in the visual spirit, which has some color and shape; still, sight does not perceive the shape, color, or appearance of its own organ. So the meeting of a perceiving power and a perceptible form does not always produce perception. The fact that one organ fails to perform a particular act of perception, while another can perform it, therefore does not prove that the powers differ.
Book Two: The nature of the animal soul, its substantiality, and its partial independence from matter
passage-en-00218

I answer that conditions and impediments are either essential and internal, or incidental and external. A difference of the first kind shows that the powers themselves differ. External, incidental conditions do not last forever and can be removed. The divine philosophy has established that the characteristic action of every natural kind occurs either always or for the most part. No natural power can be prevented from acting according to its nature for all time. If a mineral power were by nature able to perceive or imagine but never did so because a condition was missing or an impediment was present, its nature would be left without any effect. Yet reason proves that nothing in existence is wholly without effect. The same would be true if sight could perceive smells and smell could perceive visible things, but never did so because an external condition was missing or an external obstacle was present. This would make the powers and natures useless, which is impossible.
Book Two: The nature of the animal soul, its substantiality, and its partial independence from matter
passage-en-00219

As for the claim that touch and sight do not perceive the organs in which they are found, or the qualities present in those organs, that is not an essential impossibility, as the objector assumes. It is not simply something that could happen if the right condition were supplied. You already know that perception cannot be attached to a material form as it exists in matter. Every perceived form must be immaterial in some way, since matter and material things are not present to the perceiving power, as we explained earlier.
Book Two: The nature of the animal soul, its substantiality, and its partial independence from matter
passage-en-00220

Perception is not, as this researcher and those who follow him claim, a relation between the perceiving power and the existence of an external thing. Nor is sensation the presence of a sensible image in the organ of perception. Nor is it the organ’s being affected by the thing sensed outside it. That reaction only prepares the conditions for sensory perception. A living organ is affected in a particular position relative to matter carrying a certain quality. This leads the soul to take on an image resembling the qualities in that matter—the qualities we call sensible. In short, perception occurs only when the image of a thing exists in the perceiver itself, not in matter or in an organ.
Book Two: The nature of the animal soul, its substantiality, and its partial independence from matter
passage-en-00221

What shows that the powers in the sensory organs differ is this: each organ can be affected by some quality that also affects the others, yet one organ cannot bring about the kind of perception the others do. This proves that the powers the soul uses through them have different natures.
Book Two: The nature of the animal soul, its substantiality, and its partial independence from matter
passage-en-00222

The philosophers use the same line of thought to show that the animal power—that is, the power of sense and voluntary movement—differs from the plant power. If the animal power were identical with the plant power, plants would move by choice. Their bodies can move, and the power that moves by choice would be present in them. When the agent and the thing it can act on are both present, the action should follow. Plants would therefore move by choice, since there are motives in this world to seek benefits and avoid harms for bodies that can undergo opposite states. But they do not move by choice. So the plant power in us differs from the animal power.
Book Two: The nature of the animal soul, its substantiality, and its partial independence from matter
passage-en-00223

An objection is raised here: according to the philosophers, the nutritive power in one organ differs in kind from the nutritive power in another. The nutritive power in an animal must therefore differ in kind from the nutritive power in a plant. So from the fact that a tree’s nutritive power cannot produce voluntary movement, it does not follow that an animal’s nutritive power cannot produce it. What is absent from one thing need not be absent from something of a different kind.
Book Two: The nature of the animal soul, its substantiality, and its partial independence from matter
passage-en-00224

I answer that although the nutritive powers in plants and animals differ in kind, they share a general kind. Calling both “nutritive power” is not merely using one word for two unrelated things. We identify powers by their actions. If their actions have something in common, the powers do too. So the animal’s nutritive soul shares something with the plant’s, while also going beyond it through sensation and voluntary movement. It includes a further, more complete power that gives it the distinct feature separating it from plant life. Whether this general power and its distinctive feature can exist as one existence, or must exist as several, is a separate question that will be discussed later.
Book Two: The nature of the animal soul, its substantiality, and its partial independence from matter
passage-en-00225

My true view is that the soul perceives every kind of thing and produces every kind of perception; it also moves the body through every kind of natural and voluntary motion. This does not mean that we can do without the many distinct powers that mediate these actions. A higher power does not perform a lower action except through a lower power. For instance, what produces movement from place to place or a change of position must be a power spread through the body, unlike what produces movement through desire. Thought is higher than bodily extension. Any power that directly perceives must be immaterial to some degree, and the degree of immateriality matches the kind of perception: intellectual powers stand highest, while the senses—and touch above all—are lower and more deeply tied to matter.
Book Two: The nature of the animal soul, its substantiality, and its partial independence from matter
passage-en-00226

The different effects therefore come either from distinct powers with different natures or from different levels of one and the same being. Each level has a nature and effects that agree with it, whether it is separate from other levels or joined to them. Nutritive powers of different kinds share one reality, whether each is a soul in its own right, a power of a soul, or part of a soul. Touch, too, has one nature in all its forms, whether it exists independently—as in worms, whose animal soul is touch itself—or as an existential power or meaningful part of an animal or human soul. The same is true of all the powers of perception and movement.
Book Two: The nature of the animal soul, its substantiality, and its partial independence from matter
passage-en-00227

Sight, for example, may differ in kind from one animal to another, yet it has one shared reality. So do hearing, smell, taste, nourishment, growth, and the other animal powers, whether they are gathered in one power or spread among several. An example of powers gathered in one is the common sense, which brings together the five external senses. In Greek it is called phantasia. The human rational soul, though simple, likewise gathers all the powers of perception and movement. This does not mean that the organs themselves are the true sources of perception and movement, apart from the soul, except as instruments through which the soul acts. The soul itself is the sense behind all the senses and the source of intellectual, natural, and voluntary movement, because it has three levels and worlds: intellect, imagination, and sense. This will become clearer later.
Book Two: The nature of the animal soul, its substantiality, and its partial independence from matter
passage-en-00228

No one can object that if nourishment and growth were actions of the soul, then the soul would be aware of the changes and digestion it brings about. It would have to know, in detail and without learning, every stage through which food changes and every organ that food becomes part of. But that is false. So, the objector concludes, these actions must be done by a power that is unaware of what it does.
Book Two: The nature of the animal soul, its substantiality, and its partial independence from matter
passage-en-00229

The answer is not that the soul may be aware of these things but forgets them because they change so quickly—like someone who hears a long string of words spoken in rapid succession and remembers none of them. That would lead to absurdity. If we could be aware of every change in food and every bodily material into which food is transformed, without finding any awareness of it within ourselves, one might as well say that an ordinary person knows every subtle detail, even though they have no sense of knowing it.
Book Two: The nature of the animal soul, its substantiality, and its partial independence from matter
passage-en-00230

Instead, I will answer by first explaining several points. First, knowledge can be active or receptive. Active knowledge may cause its effect, or it may be identical with the effect itself. In that case, the effect’s existence is itself the cause’s knowledge of it. In general, existence is awareness, both in the cause and in the effect. This is one principle.
Book Two: The nature of the animal soul, its substantiality, and its partial independence from matter
passage-en-00231

Second, as you have learned, existence comes in degrees of strength and weakness. Its weakest forms are matter, motion, size, and number. We call something knowledge only when its existence is like form, not when it is like matter, overwhelmed and buried beneath matter’s veil. You have also learned that bodies and spatial or temporal extension mix existence with nonexistence, unity with multiplicity, and wholeness with division. This mixture prevents unified awareness and is the source of what remains unknown. That is a second principle.
Book Two: The nature of the animal soul, its substantiality, and its partial independence from matter
passage-en-00232

Third, something may be knowledge without being what is known, or it may be what is known without being knowledge. In other words, knowledge can be less complete than what it knows, which may be stronger and clearer than our knowledge of it; or the reverse may be true. When existence is supremely noble and great, it cannot be understood through some additional knowledge beyond itself, though it is knowledge of itself and known to itself. This is the case with God and the most direct intellects. Here, existence is knowledge, but it is not known by anything other than itself. By contrast, when existence is extremely low and imperfect, its image can be present to a knower even though the thing itself cannot. In this case, the image is stronger than the thing known as far as knowledge is concerned. The image that arises is knowledge; what it represents is not. In the first case, the known thing is itself knowledge, while our knowledge of it is not the thing itself but only one of its aspects.
Book Two: The nature of the animal soul, its substantiality, and its partial independence from matter
passage-en-00233

With these principles in place, we can say that even if our soul is the source of all animal and plant perceptions and movements—including attraction, transformation, and expulsion—it does not follow that it consciously knows the natural actions it carries out through matter and nature. The claim that knowing a cause entails knowing its effect is true. But when the cause’s knowledge is identical with its existence, then its knowledge of the effect is also identical with the effect’s existence.
Book Two: The nature of the animal soul, its substantiality, and its partial independence from matter
passage-en-00234

If the effect’s existence is so low and imperfect that it is almost like nonexistence, then knowledge of it is almost like not knowing it. This is what the early philosopher meant when he said that the First Intellect is ignorant of some things in a way that is nobler than knowing them.
Book Two: The nature of the animal soul, its substantiality, and its partial independence from matter
passage-en-00235

Not all the soul’s actions are like writing, walking, eating, drinking, and other voluntary acts, which require knowledge and a separate act of will. Such actions do not issue from the soul unless it first imagines them and judges their benefit to be real, whether with certainty, probability, imagination, or mistaken belief. Bodily actions, by contrast, come from the soul through its awareness of itself—which is identical with its own being—and through its love of its own perfection. This gives rise to its natural longing for what belongs to it, a longing that follows its longing for its original source. Though these points can be proved, they can be understood only by the light of inner insight and direct vision. That is why they have eluded most thinkers, and even more so those who rely on debate or imitation.
Book Two: The nature of the animal soul, its substantiality, and its partial independence from matter
passage-en-00236

One sign that the soul’s power extends through every organ, acting in ways suited to its animal, plant, and natural levels, is this: if the soul did not attend to balancing the body’s temperament and keeping its parts joined, then the slightest change in temperament—from heat, cold, movement, fatigue, or a disturbing wind—would not cause pain. Nor would events that affect the mind, such as frightening or hopeful news and warnings, affect the body. Wounds and the separation of bodily parts should cause no immediate pain either. All pain and harm would instead come only from fear of future consequences, financial loss, or punishment in the afterlife. But these conclusions are false. Illness and bodily injury hurt us at once. So the soul itself must be the subject of these sensations and reactions: its power reaches into the seat of bodily nature, making the soul itself subject to injury, pain, hardship, and illness.
Book Two: The nature of the animal soul, its substantiality, and its partial independence from matter
passage-en-00237

Even death comes upon the soul because, by God’s decree, it has entered this world. Death does not come upon the place of faith and knowledge of God and the Last Day; it comes upon the place of ignorance, darkness, motion, and change.
Book Two: The nature of the animal soul, its substantiality, and its partial independence from matter
passage-en-00238

Another sign that the soul itself, rather than an unconscious natural power, performs actions such as attraction, expulsion, and the like is that when a person urgently needs food to be transformed, digested, and expelled—as happens to a sick person at the crisis of an illness—the person finds their other perceptive powers weakened. This is because the soul is occupied and absorbed in those bodily actions, so its other actions are interrupted. Once that work is done, the soul turns again to the level where its perceptive actions take place. God knows best.
Book Three: The plant powers, their actions, and their states
passage-en-00239
Book Three: The plant powers, their actions, and their states
Book Three: The plant powers, their actions, and their states
passage-en-00240
I. The main kinds of plant power
Book Three: The plant powers, their actions, and their states
passage-en-00241

Plant powers may be powers that are served, powers that serve, or powers with a role between the two. The powers that serve the soul act on food either for the sake of the individual or for the sake of the species. If they serve the individual, they do so either to keep it alive or to bring its own growth to completion.
Book Three: The plant powers, their actions, and their states
passage-en-00242

The nutritive power alone serves the individual’s survival. It changes food into something like the substance of the body it nourishes, replacing what has worn away. The growth power serves the individual’s completion. It increases the body’s dimensions in a natural proportion until it reaches full growth. It does this by adding more than what is needed to replace what has been lost. The nutritive power serves the growth power by supplying this extra food, beyond what is needed simply to stay alive.
Book Three: The plant powers, their actions, and their states
passage-en-00243

But not every increase in a body’s size is growth. Getting fatter after the age when growth stops is not growth, and losing weight during the years of growth is not shrinking. Growth is a proportional increase that brings the body to its full development, as in youth. Its opposite is decline: a proportional decrease, as in old age.
Book Three: The plant powers, their actions, and their states
passage-en-00244

You may ask: what power causes fatness and thinness? Every action or change must have an agent that brings it about. We answer that the same power causes these changes, but under pressure from an external force. Both are forced changes. As we have already said, even in forced movement the agent is the nature and power of the thing being moved. But we use the name “nature” for a power only when it moves something by itself, not when an outside force compels it. In the same way, we call this plant power “the growth power” only when it naturally increases the body’s dimensions, not when an excess of moisture causes fatness or too much heat causes thinness.
Book Three: The plant powers, their actions, and their states
passage-en-00245

The nutritive power’s action has three stages. First, it produces a mixture that is almost ready to act and resembles the organ. Second, it makes that mixture part of the organ. Third, it makes the mixture resemble the organ in color and texture, as blood does. The process can fail at the first stage, as when food is lacking; at the second, as in dropsy of the flesh; or at the third, as in leprosy and similar conditions.
Book Three: The plant powers, their actions, and their states
passage-en-00246

The two powers that preserve the species are reproduction and formation. The reproductive power separates a portion of the final digestive surplus in the body it nourishes and gives it a power of its own kind. The formative power gives semen, after it has changed, a shape that prepares it to receive its powers and qualities by God’s permission.
Book Three: The plant powers, their actions, and their states
passage-en-00247

The powers that serve the nutritive power are four: attraction, retention, digestion, and expulsion. We can see the power of attraction at work in some organs, such as the stomach and womb; in others, we establish it by reasoning.
Book Three: The plant powers, their actions, and their states
passage-en-00248

For example, someone who is upside down, with their head below and feet above, can still drink water and swallow food. Since water and food are heavy, their movement upwards is not natural but forced. Forced movement comes either from something attracting or something pushing. In this position, pushing cannot explain how food and drink move upwards; so the stomach must draw them upward by a power of attraction within it.
Book Three: The plant powers, their actions, and their states
passage-en-00249

We also find that the oesophagus and stomach draw food in from the mouth when the body needs it. When food tastes especially good, they draw it in quickly; even the liver may draw it from the stomach because it is pleasant and akin to its nature. If someone eats one food and then something sweet, and then vomits, the sweet food comes out last. The stomach has drawn it down to its lower part. The womb behaves in the same way when it draws in semen. So does the urethra when it is empty and a woman’s desire for intercourse is strong. For this reason, some philosophers called the womb an animal that longs for semen, because it draws it in so strongly.
Book Three: The plant powers, their actions, and their states
passage-en-00250

We can show the same power of attraction in other organs. When blood forms in the liver, it contains the other three bodily fluids: yellow bile, black bile, and phlegm. Each is then separated from the others and flows to a particular organ. Unless each of these organs had a power that attracted its particular kind of fluid, the fluids could not separate by themselves, nor could each organ be supplied, for the most part, with one particular fluid. This proves that the power of attraction is present throughout the body.
Book Three: The plant powers, their actions, and their states
passage-en-00251

We can observe the power of retention in the stomach and womb through dissection. If we feed an animal wet or dry food and then open its abdomen, we find the food held tightly inside the stomach, which surrounds it on all sides. When the womb draws in semen, it grips it firmly from every direction and closes its opening so tightly that even the tip of a probe cannot enter. If you cut open a pregnant animal from below the navel towards the vulva and expose the womb, you will find it as described.
Book Three: The plant powers, their actions, and their states
passage-en-00252

We can prove that other organs also have a retaining power. Food is heavy because it contains a great deal of earth and water. It must be held in place while it is digested—a transformative process that follows attraction. This requires a retaining power distinct from the nature of food and drink, which, because they are fluid and thin, would not naturally stay in these slippery places.
Book Three: The plant powers, their actions, and their states
passage-en-00253

The digestive power changes what the power of attraction has drawn in and the power of retention has held, making it suitable for the next transformative process and bringing it to a temperament that can become part of an organ. According to those who examine the matter carefully, this power differs from the nutritive power.
Book Three: The plant powers, their actions, and their states
passage-en-00254

Here is one account of the difference. Digestion begins when attraction has finished and retention begins. When an organ’s attracting power draws in some blood and its retaining power holds it, the blood has its own specific form. Once it becomes like the organ, that form disappears and another form takes its place. The blood’s form comes to an end, and the organ’s form comes into being. This coming-to-be and passing-away occurs through cooking: the matter gradually becomes less ready to take the form of blood and more ready to take the form of the organ. The first readiness decreases while the second increases, until the blood’s form disappears and the organ’s form appears. The first stage, which increases the matter’s readiness to receive the organ’s form, belongs to the digestive power. The second, when the organ’s form is present, belongs to the nutritive power. This is the usual account of how digestion differs from nourishment in each organ.
Book Three: The plant powers, their actions, and their states
passage-en-00255

Two objections are raised. First, the digestive power changes the food’s qualities until it takes on a form like that of the organ. Whatever moves something towards an end also brings it to that end. So the digestive power brings food to the form of the organ. The larger premise is clear: what a thing moves towards is the end of that movement, and the end is what the movement is primarily for. It follows that one power produces both actions.
Book Three: The plant powers, their actions, and their states
passage-en-00256

Second, the digestive power in each organ gives the matter greater readiness to receive the organ’s form through cooking and ripening. This readiness has degrees of strength, and there is no reason to assign one degree to digestion rather than another. When the readiness is complete, the giver of forms brings the form into being. Once these actions are complete, nourishment is complete too. So there is no difference between the digestive and nutritive powers.
Book Three: The plant powers, their actions, and their states
passage-en-00257

I answer the first objection as follows. Every action of the soul has two causes: an active cause and a cause that prompts it to act. It also has two ends: the point the movement reaches, and the purpose for which it takes place. These are different ends, so they require different powers.
Book Three: The plant powers, their actions, and their states
passage-en-00258

The digestive power acts like fire: it cooks and ripens. Cooking and ripening by themselves do not mean that the process is aimed at preparing matter to receive a particular form, namely the form of an organ. The power that directs matter towards a particular purpose is different from the power that acts without such a purpose. Consider voluntary movement in an animal. One power directly moves the muscle and limb in a direction, without aiming at any particular goal. A higher power prompts movement towards something desired or away from something harmful. The first is the immediate cause of movement; its end is simply the point the movement reaches. The second is the motive power, whose end is something beyond that point: the purpose for which the movement is made, and for which the animal reaches that place. Although the purpose cannot be separated from reaching the place, it is not the same thing as reaching it.
Book Three: The plant powers, their actions, and their states
passage-en-00259
The same applies here. The power that cooks the food is different from the power that directs it towards the form of the organ, as a means of completing the individual or preserving its kind.
Book Three: The plant powers, their actions, and their states
passage-en-00260

As for the second objection, the power that gives forms to all things that come into being is indeed another source, higher than these active and motive powers. But because it is above these changes and renewals, every bodily action must also have an agent that carries it out directly. A stable agent, untouched by change, cannot directly produce these changing, renewed actions. If the recipient’s readiness alone were enough to produce movement and form, without an agent acting on it, we would not need to posit natural powers and souls in fire’s heat, water’s coldness, earth’s dryness, minerals’ stability, plant growth, and animal movement. The reactions of matter alone would suffice. But even every reaction and readiness in matter depends on the action of an agent, as we explained earlier: every ability to change depends on something already existing and able to bring about that change.
Book Three: The plant powers, their actions, and their states
passage-en-00261

Just as many different reactions cannot come from one receiver without several different aspects of receptivity, many different actions cannot come from one agent without several different aspects of activity. We have already shown in our discussion of cause and effect that a general action requires a general agent, and a particular action a particular agent. This piece of writing comes from this particular writer; this image comes from this particular artist. An observable action that we can point to must be traced to an observable agent that we can point to. An intellectual agent is not directly the agent of anything except an intelligible action. May God guide us.
Book Three: The plant powers, their actions, and their states
passage-en-00262
II. Digestion, waste, and the powers that expel it
Book Three: The plant powers, their actions, and their states
passage-en-00263

We now turn to the expelling power, distinguish these four powers, and identify the organs that serve as their instruments. As for digestion, remember that food contains two substances: one can be made like the body it nourishes, and the other cannot. The digestive power acts on each in a different way. Its action on the first is as described above. The second may be coarse, thin, or sticky. The digestive power thins what is coarse, thickens what is thin, and breaks up what is sticky. One might object: the thinner something is, the easier it should be to expel; why, then, do you count thickening as one of the changes that makes expulsion easier? We answer that a thin substance may be absorbed into the stomach wall and remain there, while a thicker substance is not absorbed and can therefore be expelled completely.
Book Three: The plant powers, their actions, and their states
passage-en-00264

The existence of an expelling power is shown by two kinds of evidence: particular examples and a general argument. First, when someone vomits, the stomach seems to be pulled upwards from its place, moving much of the surrounding organs with it. Something similar happens during a bowel movement, as the surrounding organs help expel what they contain. This is especially clear in painful straining: the force of expulsion may even pull the rectum out of place. Second, blood reaches the other organs mixed with the three bodily fluids. Each organ takes what suits it. If it did not expel what is unsuitable, that material would remain there, and no organ would be free of the diseased, harmful fluids. But that is not what happens. So an expelling power exists.
Book Three: The plant powers, their actions, and their states
passage-en-00265

Once we have established these four actions in the body—attraction, retention, transformation, and expulsion—we cannot say that they all come from one power that is merely described in different ways: attracting food as it is swallowed, holding it after swallowing, changing it while it is held, and expelling what is no longer needed. The reason is not simply the principle that one thing can produce only one effect; that principle does not apply to what is not one in every respect. Rather, these actions either oppose one another, as attraction and expulsion do, or can occur separately. An organ may be weak in one of the four and strong in another. If their sources were not distinct, that would be impossible.
Book Three: The plant powers, their actions, and their states
passage-en-00266

As for the instruments of these powers, attraction uses lengthwise fibres, retention uses oblique fibres, and expulsion uses transverse fibres. What the philosophers mean, apparently, is that the main forms of these actions require these kinds of nerve fibres. Each organ’s power of attraction, retention, or expulsion needs a nerve instrument; they do not mean that every tiny part of an organ must have its own lengthwise or transverse fibre.
Book Three: The plant powers, their actions, and their states
passage-en-00267

This answers several objections. First, the liver’s flesh has no fibres, yet the liver has powers of attraction, retention, and expulsion. Second, the eye’s crystalline humour draws in food, holds it, and digests it, even though it plainly has no fibres. Third, if every fibre were made of still smaller fibres, there would be an endless regress, yet these powers are found in them. Fourth, a transverse fibre has no lengthwise fibre, even though it attracts; and a lengthwise fibre has no transverse fibre, even though it expels waste. The reason is that these instruments are needed for the main actions of attraction, retention, digestion, and expulsion, not for every fine detail or part contained within those larger actions. The three kinds of major power act through the three kinds of fibres in the veins. Each acts directly through its own instrument, and its action extends to what lies beside that instrument, even if only indirectly. For example, when a vein draws food through its lengthwise fibres, the food passes from the vein into the substance of the liver. The same applies in the other places mentioned.
Book Three: The plant powers, their actions, and their states
passage-en-00268

You may ask: does the blood pass from the lengthwise fibres into the flesh of the liver, which is itself attracting the blood, or does it pass into the liver without the liver flesh attracting it? If the first, attraction does not depend on the fibres; if the second, the organ has no nutritive power. We choose the first. This does not mean attraction fails to depend on the fibres: it depends on them whether directly or indirectly. So every organ’s power of attraction requires fibres within it or close by, as in the liver and the eye’s crystalline humour.
Book Three: The plant powers, their actions, and their states
passage-en-00269
III. How some organs have doubled powers, and what food is
Book Three: The plant powers, their actions, and their states
passage-en-00270

Some natural philosophers may be right that the stomach has two sets of these four powers. The powers that draw food from outside the body into the stomach are not the same as those that draw from the stomach what is suitable for the stomach itself. Likewise, the powers that hold food in the stomach and change it into a substance suitable to become blood—the chyle—are not the same as those that send it to the liver. Other powers hold in the substance of the stomach the blood drawn from the liver, change it into food that nourishes the stomach, and expel its waste. The same applies to the liver: changing food into blood is different from changing it into the substance of the liver, just as turning food into liquid is different from making it part of the stomach.
Book Three: The plant powers, their actions, and their states
passage-en-00271

The more precise account is that all organs, despite their different substances, have the four powers that directly nourish them and initially produce their food. The stomach and liver have four additional powers like these, which prepare food but do not directly produce it in the first instance. Such preparatory powers may also exist in places other than the stomach and liver, such as the mouth, oesophagus, and intestines. The veins, spleen, testes, and gall bladder are among the organs that serve these functions.
Book Three: The plant powers, their actions, and their states
passage-en-00272

Know that food, in its true sense, is what replaces what the body loses by changing into the body’s own kind. Food may be potential, as wheat and bread are; or actual, when it needs no further change beyond being joined to the body. Some call it food only once it has become part of the nourished body and is actually like it.
